lesson.title: Sameness and Difference: == and !=
lesson.summary: == tests whether two values are equal and != tests whether they are different; together they are the most frequently used comparison operators in real code.
lesson.body:
Of the six comparison operators introduced in the previous section, == and != are the pair you will reach for most often, because so much of programming comes down to checking whether something matches an expected value. == asks whether two values are the same and evaluates to True when they are, False when they are not. != asks the opposite question, whether two values are different, and evaluates to True exactly when == would evaluate to False. For any two values a and b, a != b always produces the exact opposite boolean result of a == b, so the two operators are mirror images of each other.

Equality in Python compares the values on each side, not the exact type used to write them. This means 5 == 5.0 evaluates to True, even though one side is an integer literal and the other is a float literal, because Python converts them to a common numeric representation before comparing and finds that they represent the same quantity. Strings, on the other hand, must match exactly, character for character and case for case: "cat" == "Cat" evaluates to False because a lowercase c and an uppercase C are different characters.

Trace this example:

password = "mindcraft"
guess = "MindCraft"
correct = password == guess
print(correct)
print(password != guess)

Python compares "mindcraft" to "MindCraft" character by character. The very first pair, "m" and "M", are different characters, so the strings as a whole are not equal, and correct is bound to False. On the next line, password != guess asks the opposite question about the same two strings; since they are not equal, "not equal" is a true statement, so this line prints True.

These two operators show up constantly in real conditions: checking whether a user's typed password equals the stored one, whether a loop counter equals a stopping value, whether a list has reached a length of zero. Because == and != always produce a boolean value, their results can be stored in a variable, printed, or fed directly into an if statement or a while loop's condition, exactly like any other boolean expression covered earlier in this chapter.

There is one well known trap with == when floating point numbers are involved. Because computers store fractional numbers in binary, some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 actually evaluates to False in Python, even though the two sides look mathematically identical. The computed sum comes out to something like 0.30000000000000004, a tiny amount off due to rounding in binary representation, and == checks for exact equality, not closeness. Comparing floating point numbers safely usually means checking whether the difference between them is smaller than some small tolerance, rather than relying on == directly.

It is also worth distinguishing == from Python's is operator, which checks whether two names refer to the literally same object in memory rather than whether their values match; two separate lists built with identical contents are equal according to == but are not the same object according to is, a distinction that matters more once mutable objects like lists enter the picture.
